Part 2 of the guide to CAS Monograph 16, *From GLMs to Comprehensive Insurance
Pricing: Techniques and Challenges* (Chalk, Deacon, Guillen and Martinelli,
2025), the R twin of the Python guide
[`glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk-2.md`](glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk-2.md).
[Part 1](glm-to-comprehensive-pricing-chalk.qmd) covers chapters 3 to 6 and
tells which examples the guide reproduces, where the data comes from and how the
numbers are checked. This part covers chapters 7 to 10. Table and section
numbers are the monograph's.

CI runs every R chunk that has a text block after it
(`R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R`) and requires the Python guide's text. The
data are the same draws (read from `examples/data/`), and the models run on the
same Rust code with the same LightGBM parameters.

The chunk below rebuilds what part 1 built: the simulated portfolio (20,000
policies, folds from the policy number, folds 7 to 9 for testing), the
pseudo-R2 helper and cross-validation loop, the baseline GLM and boosting
formulas, the age steps that the lasso keeps, and the out-of-fold target
encoding of make (`target_encode()`, with `encode_target()` for rows outside
the training folds). Part 1 explains each piece.

```{r}
library(prospicio)

# The data files, found from the repository root (CI) or from docs/guides (Quarto).
find_data <- function(name, dir = getwd()) {
  repeat {
    path <- file.path(dir, "examples", "data", name)
    if (file.exists(path)) return(path)
    parent <- dirname(dir)
    if (identical(parent, dir)) stop("examples/data/", name, " not found", call. = FALSE)
    dir <- parent
  }
}

pf <- utils::read.csv(find_data("chalk_portfolio.csv"), comment.char = "#")
toys <- utils::read.csv(find_data("chalk_toys.csv"), comment.char = "#")
n <- nrow(pf)
pf$region <- factor(pf$region, levels = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"))
pf$power <- factor(pf$power, levels = c("low", "mid", "high"))
make_effect <- toys$y[toys$example == "make_effect"]
region_effect <- c(A = 0, B = 0.15, C = -0.2, D = 0, E = 0, F = 0.3)
true_lp <- with(pf, log(0.25) + 0.9 * exp(-(age - 18) / 6) + 0.0015 * pmax(age - 60, 0)^1.5 -
  0.08 * pmin(veh_age, 6) + unname(region_effect[as.character(region)]) + make_effect[make + 1] +
  0.25 * (power == "high") + 0.6 * (power == "high" & age < 25))
pf$fold <- (seq_len(n) - 1) %% 10
train <- pf$fold < 7
truth <- exp(true_lp) * pf$exposure

pseudo_r2 <- function(y, mu, expo) {
  null <- expo * sum(y) / sum(expo)
  1 - family_deviance("poisson", y, mu) / family_deviance("poisson", y, null)
}

# Python's list of formatted numbers: ['0.100', '0.200'].
py_list <- function(x, digits) {
  paste0("[", paste0("'", sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), x), "'", collapse = ", "), "]")
}

# Trees see region and power as the codes of their levels in alphabetical order.
tree_codes <- function(d) {
  d$region_code <- match(as.character(d$region), c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F")) - 1
  d$power_code <- match(as.character(d$power), c("high", "low", "mid")) - 1
  d
}
pf <- tree_codes(pf)
f_base <- claims ~ age + veh_age + region + power + offset(log(exposure))
f_tree <- claims ~ age + veh_age + region_code + power_code + make + noise + offset(log(exposure))
gbm_params <- list(num_leaves = 7, min_data_in_leaf = 200, num_threads = 1)

gbm_fit <- function(formula, d, rounds = 150) {
  booster_fit(formula, d, n_rounds = rounds, learning_rate = 0.05, params = gbm_params, seed = 1)
}

cells <- aggregate(cbind(claims, exposure) ~ age + fold, pf, sum)
cells <- cells[order(cells$age * 10 + cells$fold), ]
knots <- seq(20, 77, by = 3)
step_names <- paste0("age_stp_", knots)
for (a in knots) cells[[paste0("age_stp_", a)]] <- as.numeric(cells$age >= a)
cells_tr <- cells[cells$fold < 7, ]
f_steps <- reformulate(c(step_names, "offset(log(exposure))"), "claims")
lams <- elastic_net_fit(f_steps, cells_tr, alpha = 0.99, nlambda = 25, lambda_min_ratio = 1e-3)@lambda
cvp <- elastic_net_cv(f_steps, cells_tr, alpha = 0.99, lambda = lams, foldid = cells_tr$fold + 1)
kept <- knots[cvp$fit@coefficients[step_names, which(lams == cvp$lambda_min)] != 0]

expected <- numeric(n)
for (j in 0:6) {
  fit_j <- glm_fit(f_base, pf[train & pf$fold != j, ])
  expected[pf$fold == j] <- predict(fit_j, pf[pf$fold == j, ])
}
expected[!train] <- predict(glm_fit(f_base, pf[train, ]), pf[!train, ])

make_level <- as.character(pf$make)

# Per policy, the log of the make's shrunk actual-to-expected ratio: a training row in fold j is
# encoded from the training folds other than j (and other than the held-out fold), every other row
# from all training folds but the held-out one.
make_feature <- function(K, held_out = -1) {
  src <- which(train & pf$fold != held_out)
  splits <- lapply(setdiff(0:6, held_out), function(j) {
    list(train = which(pf$fold[src] != j), test = which(pf$fold[src] == j))
  })
  enc <- target_encode(make_level[src], pf$claims[src], expected[src], splits, K, pf$exposure[src])
  te <- encode_target(enc$encoding, make_level)
  te[src] <- enc$rows
  log(te)
}

cat(sprintf("%d policies, %.0f claims; age steps kept by the lasso at [%s]\n",
            n, sum(pf$claims), paste(kept, collapse = ", ")))
```

```text
20000 policies, 3659 claims; age steps kept by the lasso at [20, 23, 26, 29, 32, 62, 65, 77]
```

## 1. Highly correlated variables (chapter 7)

A GLM can split the joint effect of two near-identical features in many ways
(section 7.2), so small changes in the data move the coefficients. The
portfolio's `exper` is driver age less 17 less a small random amount:
correlation 0.997 with age and no effect of its own. The chunk fits both on each
of the seven cross-validation training sets, with and without a penalty (section
7.4):

```{r}
library(gt)
f_corr <- claims ~ age + exper + offset(log(exposure))
fits_by <- list(
  GLM = function(d) coef(glm_fit(f_corr, d)),
  ridge = function(d) elastic_net_fit(f_corr, d, alpha = 0, lambda = 0.01)@coefficients[, 1],
  lasso = function(d) elastic_net_fit(f_corr, d, alpha = 1, lambda = 0.001)@coefficients[, 1]
)
summary_rows <- lapply(names(fits_by), function(name) {
  coefs <- t(vapply(0:6, function(k) fits_by[[name]](pf[train & pf$fold != k, ])[c("age", "exper")],
                    double(2)))
  data.frame(fit = name, `age min` = min(coefs[, 1]), `age max` = max(coefs[, 1]),
             `exper min` = min(coefs[, 2]), `exper max` = max(coefs[, 2]),
             sum = mean(rowSums(coefs)), check.names = FALSE)
})
gt(do.call(rbind, summary_rows), rowname_col = "fit") |>
  tab_header("Age and experience fitted together", "Coefficient over the seven training sets") |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 4, force_sign = TRUE)
```

```text
       age min  age max  exper min  exper max      sum
GLM    -0.0540  -0.0409    +0.0340    +0.0467  -0.0072
ridge  -0.0061  -0.0052    -0.0016    -0.0010  -0.0070
lasso  -0.0074  -0.0066     0.0000     0.0000  -0.0070
```

The unpenalized coefficients change much between training sets, but their sum
(one year of age and experience together) hardly changes. Ridge shares the
effect and keeps both stable. The lasso keeps one feature, which is stable here
but can flip when the features are even closer (section 7.5.3).

For principal components (section 7.4.5), take `stats::prcomp()` of the scaled
columns and put the components into a formula like any other column.

## 2. Modelling in two stages (chapter 8)

### 2.1 The marketing discount as an offset

Chapter 8 has the only fully specified data set in the monograph: one million
simulated auto policies. Age group (A to E) and no-claims bonus (NCB 0 to 4) are
strongly related. Table 8.2 gives the policies per cell, Table 8.3 the true
relativities, section 8.1 a base frequency of 10% for age A and NCB 0. A Poisson
GLM on the 25 cells, with expected claims as response, gives the fit that the
monograph's simulation estimates with noise:

```{r}
table_8_2 <- list(A = c(132381, 54519, 12194, 1237, 26), B = c(55624, 82213, 49354, 12283, 952),
                  C = c(11053, 49903, 77029, 50248, 11291), D = c(920, 12187, 49027, 81946, 55690),
                  E = c(22, 1178, 12396, 54286, 132041))
age_rel <- c(A = 1, B = 0.7, C = 0.6, D = 0.5, E = 0.4)
ncb_rel <- c(1, 0.95, 0.9, 0.85, 0.8)
marketing <- c(1, 0.65, 0.50, 0.40, 0.20)
data_8 <- data.frame(age = rep(names(table_8_2), each = 5), ncb = rep(0:4, 5),
                     policies = unlist(table_8_2, use.names = FALSE))
data_8$expected_claims <- data_8$policies * 0.10 * age_rel[data_8$age] * ncb_rel[data_8$ncb + 1]
data_8$mkt <- marketing[data_8$ncb + 1]
data_8$ncb <- factor(data_8$ncb)
cat(sprintf("policies %s\n", formatC(sum(data_8$policies), format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")))
```

```text
policies 1,000,000
```

```{r}
#| label: tab-full-fit
full <- glm_fit(expected_claims ~ age + ncb + offset(log(policies)), data_8)
true_rel <- c(0.10 * age_rel[["A"]] * ncb_rel[1], unname(age_rel[c("B", "C", "D", "E")]), ncb_rel[-1])
gt(data.frame(coefficient = c("intercept", paste("age", c("B", "C", "D", "E")), paste("NCB", 1:4)),
              true = true_rel, fitted = unname(exp(coef(full)))), rowname_col = "coefficient") |>
  tab_header("Relativities with age and NCB in the model", "Poisson GLM on the 25 cells") |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 3)
```

```text
            true  fitted
intercept  0.100   0.100
age B      0.700   0.700
age C      0.600   0.600
age D      0.500   0.500
age E      0.400   0.400
NCB 1      0.950   0.950
NCB 2      0.900   0.900
NCB 3      0.850   0.850
NCB 4      0.800   0.800
```

The fit gives the truth; the monograph's own fit on its noisy simulation (Table
8.4) is within about 0.025 of it. Next, the marketing department's NCB scale
goes in as an offset and age is fitted again. Age relativities now increase with
age, because age carries part of the NCB effect that the offset removed. The
book's differences come from the noise in its simulation:

```{r}
#| label: tab-offset-fit
offset_fit <- glm_fit(expected_claims ~ age + offset(log(policies * mkt)), data_8)
rel <- unname(exp(coef(offset_fit)))
gt(data.frame(coefficient = c("intercept", paste("age", c("B", "C", "D", "E"))),
              book = c(0.112, 0.849, 0.925, 0.980, 1.057), prospicio = rel), rowname_col = "coefficient") |>
  tab_header("Table 8.6: age relativities with the NCB scale as offset") |>
  fmt_number(columns = book, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = prospicio, decimals = 4)
```

```text

age B      0.849     0.8485
```

### 2.2 Offsets and residuals give the same second stage

A second stage can continue from a first stage in two ways (sections 8.3 to
8.5): with the log of the first-stage predicted counts as an offset, or with the
residual (actual over predicted counts) as the response and the predicted counts
as weights. Yan and others, and Shi, show that the two are identical for a
Poisson log-link model. The chunk fits a first stage without region, then a
second stage with region only:

```{r}
tr <- pf[train, ]
tr$mu1 <- predict(glm_fit(claims ~ age + veh_age + power + offset(log(exposure)), tr), tr)
by_offset <- glm_fit(claims ~ region + offset(log(mu1)), tr)
by_residual <- glm_fit(I(claims / mu1) ~ region, tr, weights = tr$mu1)
gt(data.frame(coefficient = c("intercept", paste("region", c("B", "C", "D", "E", "F"))),
              offset = unname(exp(coef(by_offset))), residual = unname(exp(coef(by_residual)))),
   rowname_col = "coefficient") |>
  tab_header("Second stage by offset and by residual", "Region relativities") |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 4)
```

```text
           offset  residual
intercept  0.9301    0.9301
region B   1.2148    1.2148
region C   0.8598    0.8598
region D   1.0619    1.0619
region E   1.0436    1.0436
region F   1.4061    1.4061
```

In the zip code summary of section 8.4, the first rows have residuals 0 / 0.014
= 0 and 1 / 0.739 = 1.353.

Section 8.9.1 adds a caution: cross-fit the first-stage predictions, as part 1
did for `expected` in section 4.4, so that a model predicts only records it did
not see. An overfitted first stage leaves nothing for the second stage to find
(Table 8.12); cross-fitted predictions leave residuals such as 3 / 5 = 0.6 and 7
/ 5 = 1.4 (Table 8.13).

For a spatial second stage like Figure 8.2, use a `gam_fit()` with the tensor
product smooth `tensors = list(c("lon", "lat"))` and the first stage as
offset.

### 2.3 Combining tables and area groups

Section 8.7 multiplies the seven aircraft tables into one relativity for the
Cessna 172M. Section 8.9.2 replaces 30,000 zip code relativities by 100 area
groups, in equal multiplicative steps from the smallest (0.379) to the largest
(1.851) relativity:

```{r}
#| label: tab-area-steps
table_8_11 <- c(1.30, 1.15, 1.00, 1.36, 1.69, 1.00, 0.41, 0.97)
step <- (1.851 / 0.379)^(1 / 99)
checks <- data.frame(
  item = c("Cessna 172M relativity", "range, largest over smallest", "step", "range from 99 printed steps"),
  book = c(1.37, 4.884, 1.0162, 4.908),
  prospicio = c(prod(table_8_11), 1.851 / 0.379, step, 1.0162^99)
)
gt(checks, rowname_col = "item") |>
  tab_header("Sections 8.7 and 8.9.2") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(book, prospicio), rows = 1, decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(book, prospicio), rows = c(2, 4), decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = book, rows = 3, decimals = 4) |>
  fmt_number(columns = prospicio, rows = 3, decimals = 5)
```

```text
                                book  prospicio
Cessna 172M relativity          1.37       1.37
range, largest over smallest   4.884      4.884
step                          1.0162    1.01615
range from 99 printed steps    4.908      4.908
```

The printed step 1.0162 is the exact 1.01615 rounded up, so 99 steps of it
overshoot the range (4.908 against 4.884). Table 8.15 uses the rounded step:

```{r}
#| label: tab-area-groups
groups <- c(1, 2, 3, 22, 56)
gt(data.frame(group = as.character(groups), book = c(0.379, 0.385, 0.391, 0.531, 0.917),
              prospicio = 0.379 * 1.0162^(groups - 1)), rowname_col = "group") |>
  tab_header("Table 8.15: relativities of selected area groups") |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 3)
```

```text
1   0.379      0.379
2   0.385      0.385
3   0.391      0.391
22  0.531      0.531
56  0.917      0.917
```

## 3. Learning from black-box models (chapter 9)

### 3.1 The boosting model's variance

The monograph calls the gradient boosting benchmark a very complicated GLM. Its
training score keeps rising with more trees, but its validation score stops
rising (Figure 9.1). The chunk shows this on fold 0 of the portfolio:

```{r}
fit_d <- pf[train & pf$fold != 0, ]
val_d <- pf[pf$fold == 0, ]
trees <- data.frame()
for (rounds in c(50, 150, 600)) {
  b_fit <- gbm_fit(f_tree, fit_d, rounds)
  gap_train <- pseudo_r2(fit_d$claims, predict(b_fit, fit_d), fit_d$exposure)
  gap_val <- pseudo_r2(val_d$claims, predict(b_fit, val_d), val_d$exposure)
  trees <- rbind(trees, data.frame(trees = as.character(rounds), train = gap_train, validation = gap_val))
}
gt(trees, rowname_col = "trees") |>
  tab_header("Boosting on fold 0", "Pseudo-R2 by number of trees") |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 3)
```

```text
     train  validation
50   0.044       0.042
150  0.067       0.052
600  0.109       0.051
```

### 3.2 Permutation feature importance

Section 9.2 measures a feature's importance by how much worse the model predicts
held-out data after you shuffle that feature's column. The shuffle breaks the
link to the outcome and needs only predictions, so it works for any model.
Tables 9.1 to 9.4 use three insureds, frequency age / 100, a model that has
learned exactly that, and the mean absolute error:

```{r}
toy_age <- c(20, 30, 40)
toy_height <- c(1.4, 1.5, 1.6)
toy_freq <- toy_age / 100
toy_model <- function(a, h) a / 100

base_mae <- mean(abs(toy_model(toy_age, toy_height) - toy_freq))
mae_age <- mean(abs(toy_model(c(40, 20, 30), toy_height) - toy_freq))
mae_height <- mean(abs(toy_model(toy_age, c(1.6, 1.4, 1.5)) - toy_freq))
gains <- c(age = mae_age - base_mae, height = mae_height - base_mae)
for (name in names(gains)) {
  cat(sprintf("%-6s increase in MAE %.3f, importance %.0f\n", name, gains[[name]],
              100 * gains[[name]] / max(gains)))
}
cat("printed: age 0.133 and 100, height 0 and 0\n")
```

```text
age    increase in MAE 0.133, importance 100
height increase in MAE 0.000, importance 0
printed: age 0.133 and 100, height 0 and 0
```

On the portfolio, "our GLM" is the monograph's end point: the age steps that the
lasso kept, steps for vehicle age, region, power and the make encoding (at `K` =
64), without noise or experience features (part 1, sections 3.2 and 4.4). The
boosting model gets the raw features and the same make encoding, but not
`exper`: this near-copy of age would blur every comparison (the caveat of
section 9.2 about correlated features).

As in section 9.5.1, each importance is the average over the seven
cross-validation models of the loss of pseudo-R2 on the held-out fold when the
feature is shuffled. `permutation_importance()` takes a score to minimize, so
the pseudo-R2 goes in with a negative sign.

The make encoding changes with each held-out fold, so the `splits` argument
cannot fit the models here. The loop fits both models on each fold, explains
them on the held-out rows (the fold number seeds the shuffle) and combines the
seven results. It also runs `partial_dependence()` on age and the pairwise
`interaction_screen()` for the next two sections:

```{r}
veh_knots <- c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)
features <- c("age", "veh_age", "region", "power", "log_te", "noise")
ages <- c(18, 21, 25, 40, 60, 75)

# The formula builds the step columns and the interaction from the frame's own columns, so
# predict() rebuilds them on whatever frame the helpers pass (shuffled, or with age set to one value).
glm_formula <- function(interaction = FALSE) {
  reformulate(c(sprintf("I(as.numeric(age >= %d))", kept), sprintf("I(as.numeric(veh_age >= %d))", veh_knots),
                "region", "power", "log_te", if (interaction) "I(as.numeric(age < 25 & power == 'high'))",
                "offset(log(exposure))"), "claims")
}
f_gbm <- claims ~ age + veh_age + region_code + power_code + log_te + noise + offset(log(exposure))

frame <- function(mask, log_te) {
  f <- pf[mask, c("age", "veh_age", "region", "power", "region_code", "power_code", "noise", "exposure",
                  "claims")]
  f$log_te <- log_te[mask]
  f
}

# Region and power are shuffled together with the trees' codes for them.
groups <- list(age = "age", veh_age = "veh_age", region = c("region", "region_code"),
               power = c("power", "power_code"), log_te = "log_te", noise = "noise")
neg_r2 <- function(model, f) -pseudo_r2(f$claims, predict(model, f), f$exposure)
fit_model <- list(GLM = function(f) glm_fit(glm_formula(), f), GBM = function(f) gbm_fit(f_gbm, f))
imp_by <- list(GLM = list(), GBM = list())
pd_by <- list(GLM = list(), GBM = list())
screen_by <- list()
glm_with_interaction <- numeric()
for (k in 0:6) {
  log_te_k <- make_feature(64, held_out = k)
  fit_f <- frame(train & pf$fold != k, log_te_k)
  val_f <- frame(pf$fold == k, log_te_k)
  for (m in c("GLM", "GBM")) {
    model <- fit_model[[m]](fit_f)
    imp_by[[m]][[k + 1]] <- permutation_importance(model, val_f, neg_r2, groups, seed = k)
    pd_by[[m]][[k + 1]] <- partial_dependence(model, val_f, "age", ages)$mean
    if (m == "GBM") screen_by[[k + 1]] <- interaction_screen(model, val_f, neg_r2, groups, seed = k)
  }
  with_i <- glm_fit(glm_formula(TRUE), fit_f)
  glm_with_interaction <- c(glm_with_interaction,
                            pseudo_r2(val_f$claims, predict(with_i, val_f), val_f$exposure))
}

score_full <- lapply(imp_by, function(v) -mean(vapply(v, attr, double(1), "base")))
mean_loss <- lapply(imp_by, function(v) {
  setNames(rowMeans(sapply(v, function(imp) imp$importance)), v[[1]]$feature)
})
cat(sprintf("cv pseudo-R2: GLM %.3f, GBM %.3f\n", score_full$GLM, score_full$GBM))
```

```text
cv pseudo-R2: GLM 0.055, GBM 0.048
```

```{r}
#| label: tab-importance
ord <- features[order(-mean_loss$GLM[features])]
gt(data.frame(feature = ord, GLM = unname(unlist(mean_loss$GLM[ord])), GBM = unname(unlist(mean_loss$GBM[ord]))),
   rowname_col = "feature") |>
  tab_header("Permutation importance", "Loss of pseudo-R2 when the feature is shuffled") |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 3)
```

```text
           GLM    GBM
log_te   0.039  0.033
age      0.037  0.034
power    0.019  0.019
veh_age  0.011  0.009
region   0.008  0.003
noise    0.000  0.000
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-importance
library(ggplot2, exclude = "layer")
imp_df <- data.frame(
  feature = factor(rep(features, 2), levels = features[order(mean_loss$GLM[features])]),
  model = rep(c("GLM", "GBM"), each = length(features)),
  loss = c(unlist(mean_loss$GLM[features]), unlist(mean_loss$GBM[features]))
)
ggplot(imp_df, aes(loss, feature, fill = model)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "loss of pseudo-R2 when the feature is shuffled", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       title = "Permutation importance, mean over the seven held-out folds") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The two models agree on which features matter and roughly on their order. The
GBM gives the noise feature almost no importance, although it can use it. With
the monograph's treatment of nonlinear effects and of make, our GLM now scores
above this untuned boosting model (in section 1.3 of part 1 the raw-feature
baseline GLM was far below it). The GLM loss for noise is exactly zero because
the GLM does not use noise; the monograph's GLM importances are never zero,
because its lasso kept each feature in at least one fold.

### 3.3 Partial dependence

Section 9.3 isolates the effect of a feature in a black box: set the feature to
one value for every record, average the predictions, and repeat for another
value. For a GLM without interactions, the ratio of the two averages is exactly
the ratio of the feature's relativities. The printed `nu_registered` steps give
1.107 between 1 and 10; Tables 9.7 to 9.9 give the same ratio from predictions,
and the boosting model of Table 9.10 gives 1.104:

```{r}
nu <- function(v) -0.0001407 * v + 0.02936 * (v >= 2) + 0.07342 * (v >= 7) - 0.15822 * (v >= 16) -
  0.17117 * (v >= 35)
gt(data.frame(ratio = c("GLM steps, 10 vs 1", "Table 9.9, ratio of totals", "Table 9.10, GBM"),
              book = c(1.107, 1.107, 1.104),
              prospicio = c(exp(nu(10) - nu(1)), 0.01225 / 0.01107, 0.005892 / 0.005336)),
   rowname_col = "ratio") |>
  tab_header("Partial dependence ratios of nu_registered") |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 3)
```

```text
                             book  prospicio
GLM steps, 10 vs 1          1.107      1.107
Table 9.9, ratio of totals  1.107      1.107
Table 9.10, GBM             1.104      1.104
```

On the portfolio, the table gives each model's partial dependence on driver age,
relative to age 40 and averaged over the seven held-out folds, beside the truth
for a low-power car. The true young-driver effect is larger for high power,
which is the interaction:

```{r}
true_age <- exp(0.9 * exp(-(ages - 18) / 6) + 0.0015 * pmax(ages - 60, 0)^1.5)
pd_mean <- lapply(pd_by, function(v) colMeans(do.call(rbind, v)))
gt(data.frame(age = as.character(ages), GLM = pd_mean$GLM / pd_mean$GLM[4], GBM = pd_mean$GBM / pd_mean$GBM[4],
              `truth, low power` = true_age / true_age[4], check.names = FALSE), rowname_col = "age") |>
  tab_header("Young-driver effect", "Partial dependence relative to age 40") |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 2)
```

```text
     GLM   GBM  truth, low power
18  2.81  2.39              2.40
21  2.06  1.85              1.69
25  1.54  1.18              1.29
40  1.00  1.00              1.00
60  1.00  1.02              0.98
75  1.18  1.09              1.07
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-partial
pd_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(age = ages, rel = true_age / true_age[4], series = "truth, low power"),
  data.frame(age = ages, rel = pd_mean$GLM / pd_mean$GLM[4], series = "GLM"),
  data.frame(age = ages, rel = pd_mean$GBM / pd_mean$GBM[4], series = "GBM")
)
is_truth <- pd_df$series == "truth, low power"
ggplot(pd_df, aes(age, rel, colour = series)) +
  geom_line(data = pd_df[is_truth, ], colour = "grey75", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = pd_df[!is_truth, ]) +
  geom_point(data = pd_df[!is_truth, ]) +
  labs(x = "driver age (years)", y = "partial dependence relative to age 40", colour = NULL,
       title = "Young-driver effect: the GLM overstates it without the interaction") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

A partial dependence is an average over the portfolio (section 9.3), so both
models' young-driver figures mix high-power cars with the other cars. The GLM
figure is higher: without an interaction term it charges every young driver part
of the extra load of high-power cars. The next section finds that interaction.

### 3.4 Interactions from permutations

The interaction screen of section 9.4 shuffles two features separately and
together. With losses `L_A`, `L_B` and `L_AB`, the sum `L_A + L_B - L_AB` is
zero if neither feature interacts with anything, and positive if the two
interact with each other or with a common third feature. Table 9.11 prints the
three losses for three pairs with aircraft age (from the values, its columns are
`L_AB`, `L_A` and `L_B`):

```{r}
table_9_11 <- data.frame(name = c("region", "nu_registered", "faa_eng_hp_char"),
                         l_ab = c(0.291, 0.115, 0.123), l_a = c(0.253, 0.016, 0.002),
                         l_b = c(0.135, 0.135, 0.135), printed = c("0.096", "0.037", "0.014"))
gt(data.frame(pair = paste(table_9_11$name, "x aircraft age"), L_AB = table_9_11$l_ab, L_A = table_9_11$l_a,
              L_B = table_9_11$l_b, prospicio = table_9_11$l_a + table_9_11$l_b - table_9_11$l_ab,
              book = as.numeric(table_9_11$printed)), rowname_col = "pair") |>
  tab_header("Table 9.11: interaction with aircraft age") |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 3)
```

```text
                                 L_AB    L_A    L_B  prospicio   book
region x aircraft age           0.291  0.253  0.135      0.097  0.096
nu_registered x aircraft age    0.115  0.016  0.135      0.036  0.037
faa_eng_hp_char x aircraft age  0.123  0.002  0.135      0.014  0.014
```

Our sums differ from the printed values by 0.001, because the three inputs are
rounded. The same screen on the boosting model, over each pair of portfolio
features and averaged over the seven folds:

```{r}
#| label: tab-screen
screen <- screen_by[[1]][c("a", "b")]
screen$strength <- rowMeans(sapply(screen_by, function(s) s$strength))
screen <- screen[order(-screen$strength), ]
top <- data.frame(pair = paste(screen$a, "x", screen$b), strength = screen$strength)[1:6, ]
gt(top, rowname_col = "pair") |>
  tab_header("Interaction screen of the boosting model",
             "Strength of each pair of features, mean over seven folds (pseudo-R2 units)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = strength, decimals = 4)
```

```text
                  strength
age x power         0.0051
age x log_te        0.0012
veh_age x noise     0.0006
veh_age x region    0.0005
region x power      0.0003
region x noise      0.0000
```

Age and power come first, which is the planted interaction. The next pairs have
a quarter of its strength or less, and their order changes with the shuffle (the
third pair includes the noise feature, which interacts with nothing). One more
column for the first pair raises the cross-validated GLM score:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("GLM cv pseudo-R2 %.3f, with a young-driver high-power term %.3f\n",
            score_full$GLM, mean(glm_with_interaction)))
```

```text
GLM cv pseudo-R2 0.055, with a young-driver high-power term 0.058
```

In the monograph, the leaves of a decision tree fitted to the ratio of boosting
to GLM predictions did this work (cross-validated pseudo-R2 from 0.151 to
0.156). A `booster_fit()` with one tree and a few leaves is a decision tree, and
the hand-made column above uses the same idea.

### 3.5 The test data, once

All decisions above used only the training folds. By the rule of section 3.2,
the test data is looked at once, at the end. The chunk fits each model again on
all seven training folds, with the make encoding from all of them, and scores
each on folds 7 to 9:

```{r}
log_te_all <- make_feature(64)
fit_all <- frame(train, log_te_all)
test_all <- frame(!train, log_te_all)
final <- list(
  "baseline GLM" = predict(glm_fit(f_base, pf[train, ]), pf[!train, ]),
  "our GLM" = predict(glm_fit(glm_formula(), fit_all), test_all),
  "our GLM + interaction" = predict(glm_fit(glm_formula(TRUE), fit_all), test_all),
  "GBM" = predict(gbm_fit(f_gbm, fit_all), test_all),
  "truth" = truth[!train]
)
for (name in names(final)) {
  cat(sprintf("%-22s %.3f\n", name, pseudo_r2(test_all$claims, final[[name]], test_all$exposure)))
}
```

```text
baseline GLM           0.025
our GLM                0.068
our GLM + interaction  0.071
GBM                    0.064
truth                  0.089
```

Cross-validation predicted this ranking. The last digit of the boosting model
can change with the LightGBM version and platform; the last digits of the GLMs
cannot.

## 4. Challenges in ratemaking models (chapter 10)

The last chapter lists ways that a good cross-validation score can still
mislead:

- data with a misunderstood meaning (the monograph's aircraft age was the years
  since the registration certificate, not since manufacture),
- technical errors, such as factor levels coded differently in training and
  production (a fitted model keeps its factor levels, and `predict()` builds the
  design with them),
- data that breaks the assumptions of the model,
- coefficients and business mix that drift over time,
- regulation,
- outliers and data quality.

Cross-validation fails when the future differs from the folds, so monitor the
model in production. `actual_vs_expected()` compares actual and expected claims
by period, with a z-score for each period and a test for a trend in the ratio
(section 10.4).
